text: Chun-Chuan Lin
Redesigned the Save Journey, reversing a 7-month Autosave decline
For a UK savings & investing app — collapsing a two-step, wallet-mediated deposit flow into one action.
May 2026 - Aug 2026 | Research, product design
Summary

A seven-month decline in Autosave engagement reversed within weeks of launch. Daily Autosave volume held at 5–6× its prior level for the following month, and dropping the wallet vendor cut a recurring cost of roughly £10,000–20,000/month.

item: 2 steps (bank → wallet → pot) reduced to 1 (bank → pot).
Daily Autosave volume held at 5–6× its prior level for the month after launch.
After dropping the wallet vendor relationship.

text: Role: Senior Product Designer, sole designer on this workstream, reporting directly to the CEO.
The Problem
Weekly Autosave-setup volume had been declining for roughly seven months before this project started. That trend signalled something in the funding path was blocking users.

cap: Weekly Autosave-setup count, January–August 2026: the seven-month decline that first signalled something in the funding path was blocking users.

text: Diagnosis
Diagnosis without full instrumentation

Not every screen had event tracking, so I mapped the flow structurally instead: every forced wait between account creation and a working, automated pot. It asked users to complete three tasks (fund a wallet, create a pot, set up Autosave) as a strict sequence with four breakpoints, none a user could skip or work around.

bullets: KYC (identity verification) review, right after account creation: an “Under review” state that usually cleared in minutes, but sometimes asked for further documents, with no way to know in advance which outcome a user would get.
Funding the wallet before a pot could receive any money: choosing a transfer method, entering an amount, and waiting up to several hours for verification.
A subscription-plan comparison right after choosing a pot type, turning a simple “create a pot” decision into a four-tier comparison at peak friction tolerance.
A second wait once the pot existed: another deposit into the wallet, with an “arrives by tomorrow” message, before Autosave setup could continue.

text: These four breakpoints fall into two shapes. Funding the wallet and waiting for it to clear are the same wait, twice. The KYC review is a different kind of wait: uncertain, not fixed. And the subscription-plan screen isn't a wait at all; it's a business goal dropped into a task goal, at peak friction.
Together, they meant a user could do everything right and still wait a day or more for a working pot, without understanding why.
The two likeliest explanations
Two of the four stood out as the likeliest explanations, not because the data proved it, but because of what each one actually blocks.

compare: The upgrade screen users hit mid-flow

text: The wallet-funding wait was the most direct suspect: the longest real-world delay, and the step most tied to whether a pot ever got finished. The subscription-plan screen was a close second: mid-flow monetisation prompts are a well-known drop-off point, even without a log to prove it here.

I treated this as a testable assumption, not a certainty; I couldn't prove step-by-step attribution from the data. So the design addressed all four breakpoints at once: removing the wallet, deferring KYC, and clearing pot creation of the plan comparison, rather than betting the redesign on one diagnosis being right.
The Solution
One flow, two rails
After: bank → pot, directly, in one action. The wallet still exists as internal plumbing, but the user never sees it, funds it, or waits on it as a separate step.

For onboarding, I also removed the subscription-plan comparison entirely: deposit, then straight into Autosave setup, both via Direct Debit, no wallet and no upgrade prompt in between. Comparing paid tiers is a business goal, not a task goal, and has no place where a user is most likely to give up.
Open Banking made a faster default possible, but it doesn't cover every bank, and Autoinvest specifically requires Direct Debit. So the deposit flow uses a smart default rather than one blanket rule.

dd: For a one-off deposit, the system defaults to Open Banking, falling back to Direct Debit if the balance falls short, but still shows Direct Debit as an explicit choice for anyone who wants it. Most users just tap one button; the option to choose stays there for the ones who go looking for it.

text: I worked through this branching logic with AI, including edge cases like an in-flight Direct Debit payment landing after the balance check fired, before handing the specified rules to engineering.

text: Deferring KYC Until Intent Is Confirmed

Alongside collapsing the deposit step, we also moved KYC later in the flow: it now runs only after the user has confirmed the pot's deposit amount and Autosave setup, the last step of the Save journey rather than the first, and only for users who haven't already passed it. This removes the uncertain wait users used to hit right after account creation, and means we only run (and pay for) checks on users who've already committed to funding an account, letting the part they actually came for, the deposit amount and Autosave rules, complete faster.

cap: Placeholder — the decision-tree diagram above, updated with the KYC step at its true position (after both the deposit amount and Autosave setup are confirmed). Label the old position (pre-deposit) and new position (post-intent) side by side.

dd: The Autosave rules screen got simpler too, split from three simultaneous toggles (AI savings, Round Ups, custom amount) into a branching sequence: first, whether the user has a savings amount in mind (custom entry if yes, AI suggestion if no), with Round Ups, the smallest and least consequential option, moved to the end as an optional boost.

compare: Before: three toggles on one screen (AI savings, Round Ups, Custom deposit)
After: a branching sequence, savings-amount question first, then AI suggestion or custom amount, Round Ups last

text: Timeline
By mid-June, this direction was already drafted and under review. The core shape of the redesign predates what happened next.

bullets: 21 May — first Figma draft (pot onboarding flow)

text: Alternatives Considered

item: Kept an unnecessary internal account and system state alive for no user-facing benefit. Removing the wallet outright cut more steps than patching around it would have.
🎚️ One payment rail for every deposit
Routing by bank support alone broke for Autoinvest, which specifically requires Direct Debit. The right rail depends on the transaction, not just the bank.

text: The Forcing Function

We'd already scoped this as a planned migration: phase the wallet out gradually, migrate existing balances, retire it on our own schedule. Then on 30 June, our banking infrastructure partner quietly blocked the creation of new wallet accounts, with no warning. New users could no longer onboard the old way, starting immediately. The redesign had to ship for new users right away, while the fade-out for existing balance-holders continued in parallel on the original timeline.

I could have treated this purely as an outage to patch around. Instead, I used the forced timeline as a reason to fix things we already knew were wrong: collapsing two actions into one, giving every user a working funding path regardless of their bank, and replacing an accidental “front door” with deliberate entry points. The constraint didn't lower the bar on the solution; it removed the option of deferring it.
The plan accelerated:

bullets: 6–8 July — further revision covering the initial deposit and Autosave setup flow together, reviewed by another designer
12–13 August — after engineering built the flow, a QA and copy pass on the shipped build, catching UX copy inconsistencies such as “Autosave” capitalisation and “Set up” vs. “Setup”

text: Rollout
A fade-out, not a cutover
We couldn't delete the wallet for everyone on day one; some users still had real money sitting in it. The rollout split into two tracks running in parallel:

item: Never saw the wallet at all, going straight into the new one-step flow.
🧩 Existing users with a wallet balance
Kept seeing the wallet, paired with in-context messaging and a feed prompt nudging them to move that money into a pot. As each balance emptied out, the wallet disappeared for them too.

dd: The wallet had also doubled as the app's general-purpose “add money” entry point. Removing it removed that entry point along with the friction it caused, so alongside the redesign I added explicit Add money buttons directly on the Save and Invest tab home screens, letting a user fund a pot or investment account in one tap without first drilling into a specific pot.

cap: Placeholder — two-panel comparison: (1) a simple two-track diagram showing new/zero-balance users vs existing-balance users, converging once balance hits zero; (2) before/after screenshots of the Save tab home screen showing the new Add money button and the feed-prompt messaging shown to existing wallet holders.

text: Results & Economics

In the weeks following the redesign, the decline reversed: daily Autosave volume held at 5–6× its prior baseline for the following month, including a run of days that matched the app's previous busiest week of the year (early January), a signal the team read as evidence the new flow could sustain that level of activity, not just spike it.

The change also had a favourable financial shape: dropping the paid wallet-vendor relationship saves roughly £10,000–20,000/month, against a one-time cost in the tens of thousands for the banking partner to build the direct-funding API that enables Stage 2. The design case for the redesign stood on its own; the economics just made the internal timing easier to justify.

cap: Daily Autosave-setup count, June–September 2026: the pre-launch trough through June and July, then the sharp recovery at launch in mid-August.

text: Reflection
What's next

Stage 1 (shipped) was the design fix available on our timeline. It solved the user-facing problem immediately. Stage 2 (next) is the infrastructure fix: once our banking partner finishes building its own funding API, the wallet's remaining plumbing retires entirely, and we can fund the pot with no internal staging step at all.
Why this belongs in the portfolio

The interesting part of this project is where regulated financial infrastructure meets interaction design: the constraint wasn't aesthetic, it was a payment-rail and KYC/regulatory reality that had to be resolved by the system rather than exposed to the user. The forcing function (a partner cutting off wallet creation with no warning) meant the design had to hold up under a compressed, non-negotiable timeline, and be phased safely against real user balances rather than shipped as a single cutover.
